To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the time to antibiotic treatment was significantly shorter for patients in hospitals that used data feedback and benchmarking or medical record checklists to improve pneumonia care and longer for patients in hospitals in which the hospital administrator supported the intervention; (2) hospitals that used multiple interventions to improve the time to antibiotics had a shorter time to antibiotics than hospitals that did not use any interventions to improve the quality indicator; and (3) the effect of using multiple interventions was similar to the effect of using a single intervention

(1) hospitals that used data feedback and benchmarking or medical records checklists were more likely than other hospitals to administer antibiotics within 8 hours of a diagnosis of pneumonia; and (2) hospitals that used administrative support were less likely than others to administer antibiotics within that time frame.
data feedback and benchmarking, and medical records check lists were effective in increasing the time to administration of an antibiotic for patients diagnosed with pneumonia.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of quality improvement interventions in hospitals.
the effectiveness of quality improvement activities in reducing the time to antibiotic treatment after a pneumonia diagnosis.

how hospitals implement quality improvement initiatives, the effectiveness of individual and multiple interventions in improving the quality of care, and the effect of hospital size on the implementation of quality initiatives.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
data feedback and benchmarking, and medical records check lists are effective interventions to increase the time to antibiotic use after a pneumonia diagnosis.
data feedback and benchmarking, medical record checklists, and administrative support were the most effective quality improvement strategies for increasing time to antibiotic use.
hospitals should implement data feedback and benchmarking as part of a quality improvement effort to improve pneumonia care.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of quality improvement interventions can have positive effects on the time to administration of antibiotics after a diagnosis of Pneumonia.
hospitals that use multiple interventions to improve quality of care for pneumonia patients are more likely to improve the quality of pneumonia care.
the interventions that are effective in improving pneumonia care are not necessarily the interventions that are most often used.
The main takeaway from our work is that
quality improvement interventions are complex, and their effects on clinical processes may not be additive.

hospitals should consider the use of medical records checklists, data feedback and benchmarking, and administrative support when designing interventions to increase the timeliness of antibiotic treatment for pneumonia.

hospitals need to be more selective in choosing interventions for quality improvement and should focus on interventions that are likely to improve care and not on those that may be ineffective or harmful.
